entries.title: Sittin’ on the Dock of the Bay
entries.summary: Joe Kloc’s portrait of a group of outsiders living on boats in Marin County provides a record of a community many wish would quietly disappear.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
As Silicon Valley remakes the world yet again, swallowing up our water and spiking our electricity bills, homelessness remains endemic to that region of California. It is both a scandal and an illustration of what the endless speculative bubble leaves out, where the system fails—or, perhaps, what it requires: billionaires need their underclass.

Joe Kloc’s Lost at Sea: Poverty and Paradise Collide at the Edge of America tells the story of a motley group of outsiders living on derelict boats in the affluent enclave of Marin County, just north of San Francisco: an Eden of redwood hot tubs, liberal environmentalism, and, inevitably, anti-homeless sentiment. Kloc explores the contrasts between the “anchor-outs,” as they’re known in Sausalito, and the “Hill People” living above them. He also traces the connections between wealth and deprivation in the Bay Area to show how the region’s eccentric past and its serial booms and busts produced this unique seafaring community: the losers of California’s golden dream. “Among them are retired mariners, single mothers, runaways, artists, addicts, and many others who caught a bad break from which they haven’t yet recovered: a divorce, a lost job, a jail sentence,” Kloc writes. “There are those who hope their pasts won’t find them, and those who wish they would.”

Kloc offers no grand pronouncements or sweeping statements, no final-chapter solutions; this is an odd, rambling, keenly observed account, done in a minor key. Based on a 2019 Harper’s feature and bolstered by material from nearly a decade of reporting done both before and after, Lost at Sea shows us a way of life that is now mostly gone. Kloc follows the anchor-outs over the course of eight years as they spar with the harbormaster and various other authorities, navigate internal conflict, weather storms and the pandemic, get displaced to dry land for a time, and are ultimately forced out of the anchorage.

There is Larry Moyer, a ninety-one-year-old who inherited Shel Silverstein’s houseboat, the Evil Eye. Moyer, a former photojournalist for the AP, claims to have met Silverstein on the same 1957 trip to Moscow where he met Mao, Lenin, and Stalin; his boat contains multiple cats and a massive library of intriguingly labeled videocassettes. (Selections include “Sunrise,” “Dry Hump,” “Fish Head Tom,” and “Fish Head Tom Sinking.”) There is Bo, one of the only black anchor-outs, a half-colorblind painter from the Jim Crow South whose sobriquets include VanBo and Bocasso. There is Innate, a former IT worker and marine law autodidact who tosses canned tuna to the seals and gulls that circle his boat in the mornings and spends his nights researching case law to try to save the anchorage. There is Jeff, an oracular preacher who has turned the Sausalito city council podium into a makeshift pulpit, where he reads from Leviticus during meetings. (There are women on the water, too, but we don’t get as rich a portrait of any of them.) The book is full of memorable details and images: the metallic screech of impounded boats being demolished; the clementines that proliferate on the anchorage, “as common as cigarettes,” left by some local benevolent. One anchor-out tucks an egg into his breast pocket for later; another refers to death by “acute lumber poisoning”—i.e., getting whacked over the head with an oar.

Kloc is a longtime magazine journalist with a particular talent for exploring the extremities of wealth and poverty in novel ways. What Lost at Sea does most effectively is offer a picture of a homeless community that is defined by something other than simple lack. It is a firm rebuttal to the notion that people who live without traditional homes or property have, as Kloc writes, “nothing left to lose.”

Are the anchor-outs homeless, precisely? In his author’s note, Kloc expresses some unease about the term. Many of them have chosen this unconventional life for themselves and would have no other. (“It was a great nickname place down here,” Larry recollects. “The only way you found out a guy’s real name was after he croaked.”) They have a semi-stable community for Kloc to document because they are not relentlessly chased from block to block, forced to destroy their gathering places and abandon their possessions. For decades, in fact, they have been mostly left alone: the anchorage is a “jurisdictional mess,” and though the agency that oversees Richardson Bay passed an ordinance in the early 1980s limiting boats’ presence there to seventy-two hours at a stretch, it rarely enforced it.

On the other hand, Sausalito’s extreme shortage of truly affordable housing, and its unwillingness to construct any sort of shelter, means that the anchor-outs have little hope of staying in the county should they eventually desire a return to dry land. Marin County classifies them as homeless, and the more California’s homelessness crisis intensifies, the more they are interpreted and policed as such. In 2015, when Kloc makes his first trip to Richardson Bay, the city has begun to regularly seize and crush vessels that defy the ordinance. (One of the anchorage’s veteran mariners lost seven boats in his lifetime on the water.) Kloc chats up a barfly at the local joint, Smitty’s, who tells him, “When you are talking about the anchor-outs, you are talking about homeless people…people who live under a bridge in LA.”

Advertisement

Kloc’s portrait of the anchor-outs is necessarily also a portrait of the housed residents of Sausalito. Some of the hill people, like the man at Smitty’s, radiate scorn for their seafaring neighbors. Typically for Marin, there is a good deal of antipathy masquerading as environmentalism: locals are positively racked by anxiety over the fate of the bay’s eelgrass, which the anchor-outs’ moorings can damage; at one point the president of the Marin Audubon Society writes an editorial urging the community’s swift eviction. And even genuine attempts at fellowship can grate. After the death of Bo, a local fixture who lived in Sausalito for five decades, another anchor-out informs Kloc, not without some bitterness, that locals organized a show of his work to honor him. “They could have given it to him while he was alive,” he says.

Just before the start of the pandemic, spooked by a state audit that warns of “ongoing harm to the San Francisco Bay,” the Richardson Bay Regional Agency ramps up its seizure of vessels. As the anchor-outs confront the havoc left by a winter storm, a few decide to come ashore and take up residence in a waterfront park, which they dub Camp Cormorant. Soon, more join. For a while, Sausalito’s housed residents offer the camp a measure of tolerance and even generosity, donating money for toilets, a grill, and other supplies. Kloc makes a couple of passing mentions of Marin’s other pandemic homeless hub: an encampment that takes root under a freeway overpass in 2020 and that is shielded from the county’s incursions by virtue of being on state-owned land. He observes early on that the anchor-outs are nearly all white; the freeway encampment is considerably more racially mixed. For all the hill people’s hand-wringing, they also show a certain acceptance of the anchor-outs, a willingness to come into their midst, that isn’t extended to the encampment under the freeway, so much more legible as “homeless.”

Lost at Sea depicts the anchor-outs as the inheritors of an old tradition: the pilgrimage to the far edge of the country in pursuit of riches, a break with the past, or simply the unknown. Kloc is excellent on the complex interplay of will, chance, and economic reality that underlies the formation of such a community. While the 2008 financial crisis swelled the ranks of the anchor-outs, over the long term it only padded the fortunes of the hill people, with their IRAs and ever-inflating property values: “The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 had both increased over 50 percent since the eve of the financial crisis. In the same period, the number of unhoused people living on the anchorage, just across Bridgeway, had doubled.” As he camps out in Oscar Grant Plaza during Occupy Oakland, watching as volunteers struggle to provide meals amid the chaos, Kloc, who had idealized the anchor-out community upon first encounter, wonders for the first time whether it is really “the floating paradise I’d believed it to be.”

He also reaches much further back to the Coast Miwok, who lived lightly on the land, without ever needing to partition or possess it, long before it was deeded to a sea captain as Rancho Sausalito in 1838; to the prospectors who came west seeking gold but arrived too late to strike it rich and instead found themselves California’s first unhoused, living in camps; and to the devastating earthquake and fire of 1906 that leveled San Francisco and drove people to take refuge on abandoned fishing vessels in Richardson Bay. “Alas, the promised land is a myth,” one disappointed carpenter reportedly said upon arrival to the West Coast. In the years after World War II, squatters, including fishermen and returning veterans, took up residence along the waterfront—so many that, by 1951, the San Francisco Chronicle could declare: “In Sausalito people live on anything that floats.”

Then there are the children of the 1960s who went west looking for enlightenment and good vibes and wound up among that makeshift community on the Sausalito docks. Though Kloc seems to undersell the connection, this is arguably the most direct antecedent for the anchor-out community he encounters in the 2010s. A handful of his characters are refugees from that era, people with a particular orientation—toward money, toward possessions, toward the natural world, toward the balance between struggle and ease—that places them outside the bounds of mainstream American life.

A writer and Vietnam veteran named Daniel Egginck, eighty-two years old and wearing a pirate hat when Kloc meets him, boasts of dosing thousands of Marin residents with acid and takes credit for having “launched” 1967’s Summer of Love. Yarns of indeterminable veracity such as these reminded me of Ringolevio, Emmett Grogan’s account of his Haight Ashbury exploits alongside the Diggers, an anarchist street theater troupe. Grogan, perhaps more than anyone else, lived by the principle of Larry Moyer’s parting salvo to Kloc one morning: “Just write a good story. I don’t care if it’s true.” (Grogan also dated, for a time, the ex-wife of the developer who established Richardson Bay’s houseboat marina.) Amid Ringolevio’s gripes about the racial cluelessness and commodification of the hippie scene, there are some choice words for the San Francisco Oracle, the underground paper Egginck worked on, which is best remembered for its “houseboat summit” with Alan Watts and Timothy Leary: Grogan excoriates the paper for staging a “Human Be-in” on Hopi land, where hippies “committed sacrilege after sacrilege,” making love on holy ground and feeding the tribe’s children LSD.

The Summer of Love, Egginck’s purported brainchild, was what brought Moyer and Silverstein west to investigate the Haight-Ashbury scene in the first place, on assignment for Playboy. The duo discovered Sausalito’s trippy houseboat community during a trip across the bay to visit the guitarist Dino Valenti, most famous for writing “Let’s Get Together.” “There were a few hundred boats. It was total freedom,” Moyer told Smithsonian in 2012. “The music, the people, the architecture, the nudity—all we could say was, ‘Wow!’”

This spirit of stoned utopian bliss is on full display in Agnès Varda’s charming short film Uncle Yanco. Made in 1967, it features the director’s encounter with her long-lost cousin, Jean Varda, an artist living in this “aquatic suburbia.” Jean is a gentle soul, prone to statement garments and proclamations like “I am on the side of the youth,” and clearly beloved by the messy-haired young people who crowd into his boat for Sunday sails. The houseboat dwellers, he tells Agnès, “are not the sort of rebels who carry pistols—they are rebels against the system, against this American obsession with making money.”

At least, they were for a time. Jean Varda died in 1971. It doesn’t feel too far-fetched to imagine that those young hippies who visited him each week might have played their cards right, bought land, and ended up as hill people. Egginck explains, in Kloc’s paraphrase:

A lot of older Marin residents, to one degree or another, were once a part of the Haight-Ashbury scene, the Summer of Love scene, the houseboat scene. But they moved on after the Houseboat Wars, perhaps first financially and then ideologically, to make their money in the boom times of the eighties and the dot-com era of the late nineties.

Egginck continues, with the sort of enigmatic flourish that is characteristic of the anchor-outs:

“What I have learned is: every community has a Judas.”

I asked who the anchor-out Judas was.

“Hard to pin down. Every Judas has been a real estate dealer.”

There are moments when Kloc’s impressionistic technique gets a bit blurry; handing off this much responsibility for the narration can result in some blanks. We don’t get a chance to explore Egginck’s insight about the dissolution of the houseboat scene because he goes on a tangent, declaring that Moyer smuggled drugs for the CIA. From there the conversation moves to the Fukushima disaster. Kloc is too polite or averse to judgment to say that someone sounds off their rocker, so we get a lot of lines like “I didn’t know what to make of it” or “What exactly he was talking about, I wasn’t sure.” Readers may not be quite so patient.

The book’s primer on the historical forces that produced the area’s extreme housing inequality contains a few oversights. California’s tax revolution during the 1970s, which underwrote the precise shift that Egginck describes by permanently subsidizing the hill people’s homes and hollowing out the state’s ability to spend on public services, is nowhere to be found. Thanks to Proposition 13, which seriously limited property tax increases, some of Sausalito’s longtime residents may be paying just a few thousand dollars a year on homes that are now worth millions, depriving their city of funds that might have been put toward a proper homeless shelter.

Inexplicably missing, too, is a more thorough account of the so-called Houseboat Wars, which are referred to many times throughout the book but merit only a page and a half of sustained focus. In 1971 the City of Sausalito and the state-level body that controls San Francisco Bay sought to evict the houseboat dwellers once and for all. The coastguardsmen and sheriff’s deputies who came to enforce the order were met by a jerry-rigged armada, cobbled together from “a Chinese junk, a canoe, a couple of sailboats, and several rowboats, put-puts and tugs crewed by houseboat residents and their friends,” according to the San Francisco Chronicle’s archivist. The Chronicle photos from the time are remarkable: longhairs locked in battle with the cops; helmeted deputies pointing their guns at a young man kneeling on the prow of his boat, defiantly clutching a bowie knife.

The showdown seems to have cleaved the houseboat community into two camps: those, like Silverstein, who had the means to pay for berths—where today their vessels are docked alongside “million-dollar houseboats”—and those who couldn’t, who “drifted out to the anchorage.” The omission of a fuller narration of these events is an especially odd choice given that, in Kloc’s own estimation, the Houseboat Wars prefigure the skirmishes that constitute the bulk of Lost at Sea’s action. It also just seems like a missed opportunity to tell a good story.

Kloc’s work back in New York, and events like the pandemic that kept him away from Sausalito for months on end, allow only periodic glimpses of the anchor-outs’ lives. When he returns, it is often to brutal new developments. Over the course of the book at least four of Kloc’s main characters die, two of them in fires. For the anchor-outs, death is so routine that it hardly fazes: at one point, a body turns up in the water, and nobody seems too curious about who the man was or how he died.

The Covid-era move to the town park settles the question of whether the anchor-outs qualify as homeless or not. Even as the transition brings a certain ease and protection from the elements, it renders them more precarious than before. In 2022 the city offers the residents of Camp Cormorant a deal: $18,000 per person to leave the encampment for good. In the end, everyone there takes the offer. “The whole community’s been shattered—the whole tradition, the whole legacy,” one departing anchor-out bemoans. A few people get to return to their boats and stay put a little longer in recognition of their long tenure out on the water, but they know the end is coming: the Richardson Bay Regional Agency has made it clear that their final move-out date is 2026.

Jeff tells Kloc that he wants to sail to Gaza, to bring the people food. As for the rest of his fellow anchor-outs, it’s not at all clear where most of them go when they depart their longtime refuge: “They were just gone.” Whether we admit it to ourselves or not, this is the intended result of our standard approach to homelessness. “Disappearance, through force or trickery, is often the objective of policies aimed at unhoused communities,” Kloc writes in his epilogue.

Innate gets out before the forced mass exodus. In 2017, after receiving some money from the sale of his mother’s house, he buys forty acres of Arizona desert. “Years of floating on the anchorage, researching his civil rights case by the light of a solar-powered car battery, had shown him that a person’s rights were attached to owning land,” Kloc writes. “If his boat had been a house on a plot of land, for example, the harbormaster would never have been able to board it without a warrant.” It’s a concession to the values of the straight world, but it also allows him, for the first time in years, to put down roots.

Kloc’s authorial eye is not a disembodied one: he gets cold, drinks beer, must find a place to lay his head. His perspective structures what the reader has access to; we only get full accounts of the scenes he happens to be around for. And despite his lack of editorializing he is unquestionably on the side of the anchor-outs: his anecdotes show evident affection, and his choice to intersperse his main narrative with historical chapters lends credence to the anchor-outs’ claims of belonging to a longer lineage. Against a politics of disappearance, he is writing to create a record. Though the anchor-outs’ boats may be gone, something of their strange community abides. But we don’t learn much about why this story got under his skin.

I still remember reading, in 2023, Kloc’s frank reflection on the financial hardship of pursuing a career in print journalism without the ballast of family money. It’s a sort of O. Henry story, an essay about a near eviction in which he is saved from being driven out of his apartment when he receives an Economic Hardship Reporting Project grant for the essay in question. I have had a handful of conversations about it with other writers, all of whom retained the same distinct impression. Something uncommonly honest and brutal about the economic reality of this work lived within it.

Kloc writes that he first heard of the anchor-outs in 2010, soon after his arrival to San Francisco. He was then a fellow at Mother Jones. He went on to spend over a decade at Harper’s, editing serious long-form articles for an ever-dwindling audience. For this he was, as recently as 2023, paid $64,000 a year: less than when he started, adjusted for inflation. Over the same period, the rent on his one-bedroom apartment in New York increased to more than half his paycheck. He made a career in the unique and hermetic world of literary magazines just as this world was mostly vanishing. On November 13, the day I began writing this review, I went to look up Kloc’s past clips and found an announcement from earlier that day: he would be starting work at the opinion section of The New York Times. Hard to blame him for following the example of Innate, the anchor-out who sought dry land.

entries.title: ‘The Jealousy Comes from Nowhere’
entries.summary: For actors in The Winter’s Tale, the fractured marriage at the center of the play is a barometer of relationships in our own time.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Even as Shakespeare’s late masterpiece, The Winter’s Tale, continues to grow in critical esteem, New Yorkers have been able to see only five major productions of it over the past quarter-century, none of these on Broadway, where it was last staged in 1946. It returned to the Delacorte Theater as part of the Public Theater’s Free Shakespeare in the Park this past July and August, directed by Daniel Sullivan, with Raúl Esparza and Lily Rabe starring in the lead roles of Leontes and his wife, Hermione. Playgoers may also remember Ingmar Bergman’s Swedish version that came to the Brooklyn Academy of Music in 1995. It’s no surprise that The Winter’s Tale had long interested Bergman, for the play might well be subtitled Scenes from a Marriage—his 1973 miniseries exploring the decade-long disintegration of a relationship.

In The Winter’s Tale, the marriage of Leontes and Hermione is under even greater pressure, with accusations of adultery, a battle over custody, the threat of an illegitimate child, the death of a young son distraught over his parents’ strife, and the abandonment of an infant girl. It’s an unusual focus, as Shakespeare rarely wrote about the tensions of married life, especially with young children involved. When he wrote The Winter’s Tale he himself had been married for close to three decades, in a union that had survived the death of a young son and extended periods of separation. While there is much else in this play that defies easy summary, the center of attention, from beginning to end, is a fractured marriage.

Aside from the reviews that run when a show opens, tattered Playbills and fading memories are all that remain of a production after it ends. And playgoers never see it take shape—a special way to get to know a play, which I’ve profited from as a Shakespeare Scholar in Residence at the Public Theater since 2012. Early on in rehearsals this summer I was struck by how thoughtfully Esparza and Rabe were wrestling with their daunting roles. I asked if they would be willing to share their experience, and they agreed to do so; Sullivan gave his blessing.

What follows draws on conversations over the course of rehearsals and previews this summer, and focuses on the three long and gripping scenes in which the two actors appear together. As the play opens, King Leontes’s childhood friend Polixenes plans to return to his own kingdom after an extended visit. When Leontes asks Hermione to persuade him to stay longer, she does so and prevails, triggering an irrational jealousy in Leontes. Sure that she has been unfaithful with Polixenes, Leontes imprisons her and, convinced that the infant born during her imprisonment is not his, orders that the baby daughter be abandoned in the wilderness.

James Shapiro: Each of you is confronted in the opening scene with challenging speeches that will shape your characters and their fates. Lily, few lines in the play feel more contemporary than Hermione’s response to her husband’s urging her to ask Polixenes to extend his visit: “I had thought, sir, to have held my peace until/You had drawn oaths from him not to stay. You, sir,/Charge him too coldly.” When we spoke about it during the first week of rehearsals, you said that her opening words “can be playful” but also that they contained “a touch of impatience.” How have your thoughts about these first words changed over time, and what does this suggest about the kind of marriage Hermione and Leontes have?

Lily Rabe: I think Hermione has a tremendous and innate sense of freedom and moves through the world with a certain kind of ease—not that she is free sexually, but I think her nature is to be incredibly aware of everyone in the room, and to make everyone feel included. She is good at loving people, welcoming them, seeing them, making them feel seen. That line is, in some sense, a kind of tease, but it’s also the truth; it’s a test, a nudge, but a loving one, and inclusive of both Leontes and Polixenes. Even if it’s a subconscious threat to Leontes, her inclusivity can be threatening, because it is a quality that cannot be pinned down or contained.

Shapiro: Raúl, what is running through your mind when she says that—and does it feel like your marriage to Hermione is already under strain?

Raúl Esparza: Confusion. I don’t think I am being cold. I know how to speak to my childhood friend. I don’t want him to go. There’s a small sense of testing him, seeing if he cares about me as much as he says he does. There’s comfort in his being with us. Hermione and I have been distant for a bit lately, though nothing more than my usual moodiness. She’s pregnant. I’m tied to the responsibilities of the throne. I have a twinge of feeling like I’ve done something incorrectly. And that perhaps she knows my friend, and myself, better than I do. I have a fundamental insecurity about myself. Polixenes is a better man than I am. Hermione, whom I adore, is someone I am barely worthy of.

Advertisement

Shapiro: What follows may be the knottiest passage in all of Shakespeare. Raúl, can you talk about your approach and your choices in speaking these lines? Where does his jealousy come from? How do you avoid coming across as monstrous, as some actors have deliberately played him?

Can thy dam?—may ’t be?—

Affection, thy intention stabs the center.

Thou dost make possible things not so held,

Communicat’st with dreams—how can this be?

With what’s unreal thou coactive art,

And fellow’st nothing.

Esparza: The verse has been the most useful tool in approaching this passage. There is no character, there is only the language I speak. Here the scansion is fragmented. Breathing with the lines and letting them hiccup and skip almost causes me to hyperventilate. And then there he is: his panic, his racing mind, embodied in me by the words.

The jealousy comes from nowhere. Throughout rehearsals I kept trying to find the “why” behind what starts to consume me here. I discovered that it was liberating to let go of this. There is no “why.” It just is. We have all experienced irrational jealousy. It strikes suddenly. We have all then sought the evidence to support this awful pain. I know I am deluding myself. I balance the knowledge that this is “nothing” with the opposite, if I feel this “it” must be “something.” Aha, there’s the proof. It is an awful logic, but it is logical.

Shapiro: In your second scene together, Hermione is brought from prison to be tried for adultery and treason. Leontes and Hermione engage in a fierce exchange for close to a hundred lines, airing a marital dispute in a very public forum. Perhaps their sharpest exchange occurs mid-scene, when Hermione says: “You speak a language that I understand not./My life stands in the level of your dreams,/Which I’ll lay down.” Lily, could you talk about what those powerful but opaque lines mean for you?

Rabe: The words “which I’ll lay down” hold so much for me. Hermione is on trial for her life and doesn’t believe she is going to live. It is her honor she is fighting for. And tied to her honor, she is fighting to protect the truth of what her life has been, of the kind of life she has led, how she has led it—and fighting for that to exist beyond her death, and not vanish, as her life will, because of Leontes’s false accusations, his whims, his insecurity, his abuse of power. The truth of who she is—that is her legacy for her children, a “derivative from me to mine.” “The level of your dreams” to me is the thing that she has had to live so much of her life by, as she has been in a kind of fawning relationship with a narcissist—his fantasies, his fragile ego, his moods, his paranoia. All of that, which has governed so much of her life, and the lives of others she has loved, she is letting go of. She is laying it down.

Shapiro: Raúl, I love hearing your retort to her words, night after night: “Your actions are my dreams.” What is Leontes trying to convey in these five words?

Esparza: It changes every night. What you have done is my nightmare. Or: What I imagine you have done haunts me every moment of the day. I can’t stop thinking about everything you do and everything you may have done. I can’t stop obsessing over who you really are, who I thought you were. Or: Polixenes has fled. The child exists. I am not imagining these things. A veil has lifted, and I see clearly now through my previous happy dream.

Shapiro: The Delphic oracle confirms Hermione’s innocence. But she collapses at trial’s end when news arrives that their young son, Mamillius, has suddenly died. Sixteen years pass. A penitent Leontes, who believes his wife is long dead, refuses to remarry. And in the play’s final scene, he and his long-lost daughter Perdita are invited by Paulina to see a recently finished statue of Hermione. They, and we, watch as it comes to life. (Shakespeare is ambiguous here about how supernatural Hermione’s return to life might be, making it appear magical and having Paulina invite all to “awake your faith,” but also hinting at more plausible explanations.)

The text remains unclear about the extent to which they then reconcile. For most of the play’s stage history, productions ended in the couple’s warm embrace—until the Hermione of Lillah McCarthy was likely the first to break with that tradition at the Savoy Theatre in 1912. How has your thinking about this moment changed during rehearsals?

Esparza: Lately I have noticed a constant repetition of the words “affliction” and “grace” in the play. Every character is afflicted. Every character receives grace. I don’t think of this as a moment of reconciliation. I think of it as a moment of grace. Grace is unearned. It comes from outside of us. I am given grace by the extraordinary Paulina; there is so much love for Hermione and Leontes in her actions. I am given grace by the presence of Polixenes and Camillo. And then there is the magnificence of my daughter restored to us, also by inexplicable grace. This suggests to me that the winter is ending, there is a break in the clouds. It contains possibility, but it doesn’t contain resolution.

Rabe: As far as what is ahead for Hermione and Leontes, it is just the beginning of a new life, and I think it is living with the uncertainty, the enormous risk in beginning again, that is most important and most tangible.

Shapiro: Opening night is fast approaching, and I imagine your choices are close to locked in. As the play draws to an end, Hermione briefly takes both Leontes and Polixenes by the hand before letting go of both and embracing Perdita. What are you experiencing in that final moment?

Rabe: To me, the thing that keeps Hermione alive, or brings her back to life, however an audience member wants to look at it, is the hope—not the guarantee—that her daughter remains living. That is enough. It would be enough for sixteen years, it would be enough for a hundred years. The one thing I know about the next chapter of my life is that I will be with and get to know my daughter. And with her comes the memory of my son, who will always be with me. I get to have my beloved friend Polixenes back. I also get to be with Paulina, who has helped to keep me alive, and given me hope; the bond between those two women is indescribable.

Esparza: Nothing is ever locked in. Staging may be set, but every performance is different because the audience (or the sky or the sounds of the city) finishes the work with you. And with Lily, who is a truly great actor, every night I find something new in the scenes we share. Recently, when she takes my hand, it has been a feeling that I am seen and the door is open to come to her. When Hermione lets go and embraces our daughter, I feel a breath lifting in me. In that breath, something broken is beginning to mend.

entries.title: Unraveling Medical Mysteries
entries.summary: Patients with undiagnosed conditions suffer not only from their symptoms but also from the uncertainly of not knowing what afflicts them.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Patients without a diagnosis live in a medical purgatory. Their failure to receive one may be attributed to their having vague symptoms, such as a general feeling of malaise, weakness, or fluctuating muscle pain. They usually consult their primary care doctor, who, unable to provide a diagnosis, refers them to specialists: neurologists, gastroenterologists, rheumatologists, hematologists, cardiologists. Desperation fills their lives, amplified by physicians who dismiss their complaints as psychosomatic—in their heads—and then prescribe medications for mental health conditions, such as Prozac or Valium. Not infrequently, when a person’s symptoms are seen as manifestations of stress and anxiety, Alexandra Sifferlin writes in her engaging and illuminating The Elusive Body, it makes “getting a diagnosis deeply complicated and rife with uncertainty.” Doctors often retreat from continuing to care for such patients, frustrated that despite a physical exam and blood tests and scans they are unable to offer an answer. And without one, treatment becomes guesswork, ineffective at best, harmful at worst. Patients without a diagnosis typically feel they have exhausted every resource and don’t know where to turn.

The centerpiece of The Elusive Body is the Undiagnosed Disease Program (UDP) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). It serves, Sifferlin writes, as “a clinic of last resort,” bringing together a team of physicians and researchers who try to unravel a patient’s mysterious condition by applying advanced technologies, particularly genetic analysis. They don’t always succeed in providing an answer, but when they do, even in the absence of an effective therapy, there is meaningful relief for patients who learn it’s not all in their heads.

The plight of Louise Proctor, a woman with an undiagnosed malady, spans many pages in the book and poignantly illustrates the physical and psychological vicissitudes of life in medical purgatory. Her odyssey began in 1980, when she was twenty-five and working full-time in a family services office in rural Kentucky. Her job, entering data into spreadsheets from food stamp and welfare applications, was mostly sedentary. One lunch break she found that she could hardly climb a familiar hill. The pain began in her toes and moved up her legs: “When she bent down to massage the muscle in her left calf, she nearly cried out in agony. Her leg felt as hard as a rock.”

In the ensuing years, such episodes occurred frequently. Her legs felt as though they were “turning to stone,” and as her condition worsened, her strength waned. Louise consulted numerous physicians. She was told that her leg pain was caused by insufficient exercise, possibly by arthritis, or even by secondhand smoke. But despite her exercising more, eating well, and taking prescribed medications for arthritis, her symptoms did not abate. Outwardly nothing seemed wrong with her legs. Repeatedly told that she just needed to walk more, she felt that her condition was being attributed to her sloth. “I knew something was wrong,” she told Sifferlin in a later interview. “I wasn’t imagining it.” For three decades, as her legs repeatedly froze, Louise did not receive a diagnosis. “The mystery deepened when her four siblings also began experiencing similar symptoms,” Sifferlin writes.

Louise’s life became even more fraught when her baby daughter, Suzanne, didn’t gain weight. Initially, as in Louise’s case, there was no diagnosis, but then the two of them went to a medical center in Lexington, Kentucky, and Suzanne was told she had cystic fibrosis. This is a genetic disorder that affects the transport of ions such as chloride in vital tissues, including the lungs, pancreas, and intestines. Mucus builds up, impairing breathing and damaging organs.

“These two Proctor women exemplify just how powerful a diagnosis can be,” Sifferlin writes.

Suzanne’s awful symptoms and poor prognosis were at least explained. With that certainty, she and her mother could see what lay ahead, and that clarity gave Suzanne a kind of peace. It also focused her doctors’ efforts: Having a diagnosis meant Suzanne’s medical team knew what they were dealing with, and what treatments they could try. Louise, meanwhile, was languishing without one.

Suzanne died at the age of fifteen. After her death, Louise decided “to confront the mystery of her own body once more.” She eventually saw Dr. Karen Saylor, a family physician, who listened attentively as she described how she could not do daily chores such as laundry, walk up a driveway, or keep up with her family on a visit to a zoo. Dr. Saylor sent Louise to the hospital for imaging. It had been many years since she had stood frozen in pain on that familiar hill, and this was the first time a doctor had ordered imaging (which shows how glibly her complaints had been dismissed). The result of the ultrasound “was shocking: Louise’s arteries all around her knee were lined with hardened calcium.” She thought to herself, “I’ve been trying to tell everyone something was wrong, and no one would listen.”

Advertisement

A doctor’s ego may be an obstacle to admitting being stumped in making a diagnosis. Dr. Saylor, on the other hand, was willing to acknowledge that she was clueless after the ultrasound and sought help to find answers. She found that there was a team of physicians and researchers “who focused on the most complex medical cases that baffle physicians across the United States”—the UDP—and she sent Louise’s and her sister’s medical histories, the ultrasound and X-rays, and other records to the NIH.

The UDP had been open for only a year when Dr. Saylor reached out to its director, Dr. William Gahl, a pediatrician and geneticist who focused on rare diseases and had been the clinical director of the National Human Genome Research Institute of the NIH. “People with rare diseases feel the limits of the diagnostic process most acutely,” Sifferlin notes. Because these patients have diseases that are less familiar to health care professionals, they often end up languishing for long periods without a diagnosis or are misdiagnosed and receive incorrect treatments. The UDP was founded not only to provide answers to patients who had sought diagnoses for years; it also reflected the NIH’s primary research mission by discovering new diseases, launching clinical trials, and connecting patients with others who share a rare disorder. (The UDP was ultimately expanded to the Undiagnosed Diseases Network—UDN—to include academic centers beyond the NIH, particularly those with expertise in genetics, such as Harvard and Baylor.)

The UDP was the first resource of its kind in the United States. It was launched in May 2008 and in the first two weeks more than two hundred prospective patients called; it since has received thousands of applications. How to triage these applications was a challenge. Dr. Gahl said that his team was looking for clues from the patients’ stories, physical examinations, and laboratory tests, in search of “a new, unique, or remarkable physical finding or constellation of such findings.” A medical board of NIH experts reviewed the cases and then invited selected patients for a weeklong visit, during which they would undergo testing and be seen by a team of specialists in different disciplines. To be admitted to the program, the applicant “didn’t just have to be sick and not know why,” Sifferlin writes. “Their illness had to be unique enough to go undiagnosed, while also potentially bearing on a more widespread health problem.”

Louise Proctor’s case was new to Dr. Gahl and his colleagues. They had never seen X-rays and ultrasound images that showed deposits of calcium as extensive as those in her and her siblings’ limbs. Blood was reaching Louise’s legs only through collateral vessels that had developed to bypass the blockages and were too limited to allow blood to flow normally, thus causing severe pain and limited mobility.

The fact that Louise’s four siblings were experiencing similar symptoms, Sifferlin writes, “suggested a possible genetic link.” The UDP’s geneticists were uniquely suited to explore their mysterious malady. In May 2009 the entire Proctor family gathered at the headquarters of the UDP in Bethesda, Maryland. “By this point,” Sifferlin notes, “all five siblings struggled to walk more than one to six blocks without pain.” They underwent an extensive evaluation, including X-rays, PET scans, CT scans, ultrasounds, and, most critically, genetic analysis. The sequencing of the human genome had been completed by 2003, and in 2009, as Dr. Gahl was reviewing the Proctors’ application, there was a push to sequence the DNA of more people to better understand genetic variation and illness. The Proctors were accepted into the UDP.

“A healthy person’s blood vessels should look like a garden hose,” Sifferlin writes. “But the blood vessels of Louise and her siblings were shockingly obstructed by calcium.” As it happened, a vascular specialist at the NIH had a postdoctoral fellow, Dr. Cynthia St. Hilaire, working in his laboratory. After seeing Louise’s CT scan, “she felt a twinge of recognition.” Dr. St. Hilaire had done her Ph.D. work on a protein called the adenosine receptor. One of its functions is to control the constriction and relaxation of blood vessels. Her studies included genetically engineered mice that allowed the researchers to see the function of the protein by deleting the gene. The mice without the adenosine receptor had characteristics that resembled what Dr. St. Hilaire saw in the Proctor siblings’ legs. “It seemed far too serendipitous that her incredibly narrow area of Ph.D. research would apply to her first case acting as a consultant for the UDP,” Sifferlin writes. The members of the Proctor family each underwent a skin biopsy that extracted from their arms a small piece of tissue about the size of a pencil eraser for further laboratory study.

Advertisement

Both Proctor parents were healthy. Each presumably had one copy of the mutated gene and one copy of the intact gene, which indicated that the trait was recessive. But “each of their children may have inherited two copies of the mutated gene, one from each parent, which resulted in their symptoms.” The UDP team learned that the parents were third cousins, increasing the likelihood that they shared a recessive mutated gene.

The team initially identified ninety-two genes that they suspected could contain the sought-after mutation. Dr. St. Hilaire examined the list and saw a gene for CD73. “She was shocked because CD73 is the main enzyme that produces adenosine, the molecule that binds and activates the receptor she had studied during her Ph.D. program.” When the researchers analyzed the proteins from the skin cells, they found that the Proctor siblings had no CD73. “Holy shit, holy shit, holy shit,” Dr. St. Hilaire whispered to herself. “There’s no CD73 there.” It turned out that a gene responsible for producing CD73 was mutated. The team could now definitively say that the lack of CD73 was the cause of calcium deposits in the Proctor siblings’ arteries. “This was the answer. It was a truly novel disease discovery,” Sifferlin writes.

The UDP identified nine people who had the mutation and similar symptoms: the five Proctor siblings, three sisters in Italy, and one person in San Francisco. The researchers named the condition arterial calcification due to deficiency of CD73 (ACDC). The findings were published in The New England Journal of Medicine in February 2011.

For the Proctor siblings the findings afforded an understanding of what was afflicting their bodies. “It was all a bit mind-blowing,” said Louise’s sister Elizabeth. “It’s nice to know why I am having this pain, and that it’s not because I am out of shape. I am not crazy and there is a medical reason for this.” After decades of appointments and being dismissed, this was a true diagnosis. Although there is not yet a specific therapy for ACDC, simply knowing what is wrong moves a patient out of purgatory as scientists work on finding an effective treatment.

A few years later Dr. St. Hilaire published a study showing that the kind of calcification experienced by the Proctor siblings is a more serious form of the calcification experienced by millions of people with more common peripheral vascular disease. ACDC involves calcification of blood vessels and although rare is relevant to patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and hypertension who also suffer disabling vascular impairment. An estimated eight million people forty and older in the United States have a related condition. “That’s one thing people don’t fully appreciate,” said Dr. St. Hilaire. While the Proctor calcification is rare and aggressive, Sifferlin writes, “the underlying mechanisms are shared among people with less severe but still debilitating artery disease—they also have low CD73.” Dr. St. Hilaire’s laboratory is hoping to use the knowledge gained from the UDP discovery to treat other vascular diseases.

Patients who are incorrectly diagnosed occupy a parallel purgatory to those without a diagnosis, because they also lack an accurate picture of their disorder. Their symptoms, like those of patients without a diagnosis, persist as doctors prescribe ineffective or harmful therapies. Between 10 and 15 percent of all patients are estimated to be misdiagnosed or suffer a serious delay in diagnosis. Some of these data come from studies that found that the true cause of the disorder was revealed only by an autopsy.

Sifferlin touches on the cognitive pitfalls that can result in misdiagnosis. The work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in identifying and characterizing heuristics and biases, which often occur under conditions of uncertainty and time pressure—both prevalent in medicine—can explain much of flawed clinical reasoning. Dr. Pat Croskerry, an emergency room physician in Nova Scotia who has a Ph.D. in psychology in addition to his medical degree, developed a catalog of biases in medicine. For example, doctors may seize on the first symptom offered by the patient or the first abnormal laboratory finding—so-called anchoring—and then follow a path of thinking that ignores other salient information. Anchoring fixes the physician’s mind on a single diagnosis that all too often is wrong. Another common bias is known as availability. Here the physician’s thinking is guided by what is most available in their mind, often a dramatic case or a recent series of similar patients, as in the midst of a flu epidemic. In such cases the physician ignores the alternative diagnoses that should be considered.

A third kind of misguided thinking is attribution bias: the tendency to blame people rather than circumstances when things go wrong, for example by invoking negative stereotypes. A disheveled man, unshaven, with an enlarged liver, may be designated a drunk with alcoholic cirrhosis, although in fact he has an inherited liver disorder and does not drink to excess.

While working on my book How Doctors Think (2007), I had the opportunity to interview scores of patients and physicians in an effort to illustrate each of these cognitive biases with real-world cases. I recount in my writing several of my own misdiagnoses when I fell into cognitive traps. As a resident in training, I saw an elderly woman with diabetes who complained of abdominal pain. I anchored on gastroparesis, a slowly emptying, bloated stomach, which is a common diagnosis in diabetics. I missed the serious underlying cause of her pain: an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Fortunately she survived my mistake.

Sifferlin briefly mentions how to protect against some cognitive biases. She raises the question inherent in metacognition—thinking about your thinking—that clinicians should pose to themselves: What else could it be? But it’s important to ask whether there are any data from the patient’s history, physical exam, laboratory testing, X-rays, and scans that do not fit into the working diagnosis. Moreover, it is also important to question Occam’s razor, taught in medical training, which posits that there should be a single unifying hypothesis that accounts for a constellation of findings. Human biology does not conform to such a paradigm of logic, since often there is more than one cause for diverse symptoms. This protects against doctors stopping their thinking when they find the first diagnosis; if they are too satisfied in their search, they miss a second possible diagnosis or even a third.

After Donald Trump took office for the second time in January 2025, he and the Department of Government Efficiency, initially headed by Elon Musk, began cutting federal funding for scientific and medical research, including for the NIH. There was concern that the UDN could be closed down, Sifferlin writes:

The saving grace has been the patients. They’ve formed advocacy groups and worked hard to keep the program running, including calling on members of Congress. The goodwill the US government earns from taking medical mysteries seriously is hard to overstate. UDN has successfully diagnosed hundreds of Americans, and it builds trust in a health system that badly needs it.

While the program is focused on rare and undiagnosed diseases,

it has become a model for how to approach difficult diagnoses broadly. It emphasizes teamwork, deep dives into each person’s medical history, and long appointments that combine cutting-edge science with the trust-building elements of good bedside care.

There is a certain irony here, since the UDN draws on the most advanced medical technologies—detailed genetic analysis, sophisticated scans, comprehensive blood tests. But as Louise Proctor’s case showed, unraveling a medical mystery begins in the old-fashioned way—by taking the patient seriously.
